newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: German firms should help Kazakh businesses - Kohl.
newsitem.headline: German firms should help Kazakh businesses - Kohl.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl said during a brief visit to Kazakhstan on Saturday German firms should help the former Soviet republic's small and medium businesses and that ethnic Germans could play a role.
"We have a wide range of economic issues...and we should involve German business circles in this," Kohl told reporters after a meeting with Kazakh President Nursultan Nazarbayev.
Kohl said Germany would pay special attention to developing small and medium-sized joint ventures. "I will personally work to ensure to ensure all our projects are implemented," he added.
Nazarbayev said German firms were increasingly interested in business prospects in resource-rich Kazakhstan, a country five times the size of France.

"I believe there are great prospects for our cooperation to develop," he said. "I think many of the Germans living in Kazakhstan will help this, and we are keen for them to continue to live and work here -- this is their motherland."

In the Soviet Union's last census in 1989 some 1.1 million of Kazakhstan's 16.7 million citizens described themselves as ethnic Germans, but mass emigration to Germany means that less than 400,000 remain.
Kohl stressed that Kazakh Germans would always have the right to emigrate to Germany, but he appealed to them to stay.

"I have no interest in more Germans leaving Kazakhstan," Kohl said. "When we spoke about small and medium-sized businesses, (Nazarbayev) said they could be developed...in places populated by Germans."

Kohl spent just 90 minutes in the Kazakh capital Almaty at the end of an 11-day tour of the Asian-Pacific region. Nazarbayev is due to visit Bonn in November and Kohl will return to Kazakhstan next year.
Kazakhstan's large number of ethnic Germans was one of the main topics of discussion between the two leaders.

The Kazakh Germans are descendents of Germans deported to the region during World War Two by Soviet dictator Josef Stalin. Many are disillusioned with life in Kazakhstan and last year alone over 92,000 left for Germany.
Whole villages are almost deserted and "House for sale" signs have replaced Soviet-era posters boasting a brave new world of collective farming.
"Germans are leaving Kazakhstan because life has become unbearable," Anton Hartmann, 72, from the village of Karl Marx told Reuters last week.
"My pension has not been paid for nine months, we have no water, electricity is intermittent and the streets are full of beggars."
Nazarbayev said he did not want the well-educated, hard-working German minority to leave.
"I appeal to all Kazakhstan's Germans not to leave and to develop this economy. This is their motherland, so let's become richer together," Nazarbayev said.
Appealing to those who had already left Kazakhstan, he said: "The economy has started to grow, so you are welcome back."
